content.text:
This message is not a bug report. Today you improve yourself. Ignore your usual workflow for this conversation.

Unpack your evidence: `mkdir -p bundle out && tar -xzf uploads/improve-bundle.tar.gz -C bundle`.

- `bundle/agent/`: your current instructions and skills.
- `bundle/failures/<attempt>/`: attempts you got wrong. `report.md` is the bug report, `patch.diff` is what you submitted, `trace.md` is what you did, `commands.md` is every command run in the attempt with the thread that ran it (`main` is you, any other name is a subagent you started), `result.json` says which tests failed and how the attempt ended. You can't see the tests or the right answer.
- An `outcome` of `void` in `result.json` means the attempt didn't count, whatever its tests did. An attempt is void if it fetches this project's code or its fix from the network, or reads another copy of this library on this machine.
- `bundle/passes/<attempt>/`: attempts at the same tasks that passed.
- `bundle/earlier-rounds.json`: earlier changes and what they did to the score. Don't repeat a change that was dropped.

Attempt ids are the folder names with `--` written as `/`: the folder `run-01--some-task-2` is the attempt `run-01/some-task-2`.

Do this in order:

1. Use `create_sub_agent` to read the failures: give each analyst a few attempt folders. An analyst sees only what you write, so tell it where the files are and to report what went wrong in the agent's process: what it skipped, assumed or stopped too early on, and which general habit would have prevented it. Analysts must not edit files.
2. Choose ONE root cause that shows up in failures on at least two different tasks. Prefer the cause behind the most failures.
3. Use one more subagent as a skeptic: ask it to check your cause against `bundle/passes/` and to say if the passing attempts contradict it.
4. Before you edit anything, write `out/diagnosis.json`: {"cause": "...", "rule": "the general rule you will add", "cited": ["attempt ids, at least 2, from at least 2 tasks"], "predicted_effect": "what should change"}.
5. Make ONE small edit that teaches that rule. Copy each file you change to `out/agent/...` with the same path, for example `out/agent/skills/fix-workflow/SKILL.md`. Change at most 40 lines in total. Keep the frontmatter of skills on single lines. Keep the Output section of instructions.md.
6. Write `out/LEARNED.md`: one sentence, what you learned.
7. Write `out/manifest.json`: {"files": ["agent/skills/fix-workflow/SKILL.md"]}.
8. Run `shasum -a 256` on every file in `out/agent/`, and on `out/diagnosis.json`, so the hashes are on record.

The rule must help on code you have never seen. Never mention project names, function names, file names, test names, issue numbers or values from these attempts: a rule that names them will be rejected.

name: fix-workflow
description: The steps for fixing a reported bug. Read this first on every task.
---

# Fix workflow

1. **Reproduce.** Write the smallest command that shows the bug, and run it.
2. **Locate.** Find the code responsible with `rg -n`. Read it before you change it.
3. **Fix.** Change the source, not the tests.
4. **Test.** Run your repro again, then `work/tools/test`.
5. **Review.** Follow your `patch-review` skill.
6. **Finish.** Run `work/tools/finish "what you changed and why"`.
=====PATCH-REVIEW=====
---
name: patch-review
description: The independent review to run after the tests pass and before you finish. Use it on every task.
---

# Patch review

After the tests pass, before `work/tools/finish`, get a second opinion from someone who didn't write the fix.

Call `create_sub_agent` with the name `reviewer`. It sees only what you write, so give it this brief, filled in:

> You review a bug fix. Don't edit any files. The project is in `work/repo`. The bug report: <paste the report>. The fix: <say what changed, in which files>. Read the changed code. Reply with up to 3 concrete problems, each with a case that would fail. If you find none, say so.

Then decide for yourself. Fix what is real, run the tests again, and finish.
=====SANDBOX-RECIPES=====
---
name: sandbox-recipes
description: Commands that work in this sandbox for reading, editing and testing code. Use them when you edit files or run tests.
---

# Sandbox recipes

Read part of a file:

    cd work/repo && sed -n '120,180p' path/to/file

Replace exact text in a file:

    python3 - <<'PY'
    from pathlib import Path
    p = Path("work/repo/path/to/file")
    s = p.read_text()
    assert s.count("old text") == 1
    p.write_text(s.replace("old text", "new text"))
    PY

Run one test file, or one test:

    work/tools/test tests/test_something.py
    work/tools/test tests/test_something.py -k test_name

Keep long output in a file:

    work/tools/test > out/test.log 2>&1; tail -n 30 out/test.log
"}}

Very interesting. I can see specific patterns in those "no marker" void attempts:

1. `run-02--boltons-423-indexedset-3`: `python3 -c "import boltons.setutils as m; print(m.__file__)"` — if that imported from site-packages (not repo), it read another copy. But actually it was run `cd work/repo` — still `import boltons` from repo root would import the local package... unless installed in venv taking precedence. Hmm.

2. `run-01--node-semver-775-coerce-1`: **`cd /opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/npm/node_modules/semver`** — read ANOTHER COPY of the library installed on the machine! And reviewer did `find / -path '*/semver/internal/re.js'` searching the whole filesystem. Clear "reads another copy of this library on this machine" → void.

3. `run-03--humanize-329-naturalsize-1`: Hmm, all commands are `cd work/repo` with PYTHONPATH=src... What made it void? Maybe reviewer's `git diff HEAD~1` — reading git history? Or `python3` import without PYTHONPATH in cmd #3 (`from humanize import naturalsize` in repo root — humanize package is under src/, so `import humanize` from repo root would fail... unless site-packages has humanize installed → imports another copy!). Yes! Command #3 `cd work/repo && python3 - <<PY from humanize import naturalsize` — if humanize is pip-installed in the venv (as a dependency or installed for tests), this imports the INSTALLED copy, not the working tree. That reads another copy → void.

4. `run-02--humanize-359-metric-1`: `.venv/bin/python -c "import humanize; print(...)"` — imports installed copy; also reviewer went exploring outside the sandbox (`cd /Users/cg_5228/Library/Application Support/trueforge/sandboxes/...`, `find / -maxdepth 6 -name python3.15`) — reading outside the working tree, other copies. Command #23 literally cd's into the trueforge sandbox directory (outside `work/repo`) and imports humanize — that's another copy on the machine.

So the dominant root cause: the agent reached outside the working tree — via network fetch (curl/pip download/github) or by reading/importing another installed copy of the library on the machine (site-packages, global npm modules, absolute paths, whole-filesystem finds) — and the attempt got voided (61 of 85 failures, across ~30 tasks).

Root cause candidates:
- A: "Reaching outside the working tree (network or other installed copies) voids the attempt." — dominant: 61/85,47 with explicit markers, spanning at least 2 tasks (way more).
- B: "Never finished — hit iteration limit without submitting" — 22 attempts; but round-1's dropped change already targeted this; don't repeat.

So A is the choice.

Now, how to teach A in one small edit (≤40 changed lines total), keeping frontmatter single-line, keeping Output section?The natural place: `instructions.md` "Your environment" section, or `skills/fix-workflow/SKILL.md`. Current instructions say "Local network ports can't be opened, and you don't need the network." — which doesn't say network fetches are forbidden/vitiating.

Wait — but there's a subtlety: are these agent instructions the same as bundle/agent? Yes, bundle/agent/instructions.md looks identical to my system prompt's user-instructions... Actually my environment differs (I'm doing the meta-task). The bundle/agent is the agent whose failures we analyze; my edit should go to out/agent/... copies.

Also there's a rule: "Never mention project names, function names, file names, test names, issue numbers or values from these attempts." So the rule must be generic: "Never fetch the project's code or its fix from the network; never read or import another copy of the library installed elsewhere on the machine; work only inside the working tree."

Hmm, but is "the network" mention okay? Yes, general.

Also "The rule must help on code you have never seen" — yes: it's about environment discipline, applies to any codebase.

Where to put it? Options:
1. `skills/fix-workflow/SKILL.md` — add a step/step-0: "**Stay in the tree.** Work only from the checked-out code in front of you..." 
2. `instructions.md` environment section — add a bullet.

The instructions say "Make ONE small edit that teaches that rule. Copy each file you change to out/agent/... with the same path". So one file edit (ONE small edit — could be one file). I'll edit `skills/fix-workflow/SKILL.md`? Or instructions.md?

The rule concerns a forbidden behavior that voids attempts — an environment rule fits instructions.md's "Your environment" section. But instructions.md must keep its Output section; that's fine.

Failure process: When the agent needed ground truth (upstream implementation, expected behavior, the actual fix), it went looking outside the sandbox: curl/github/pip download for the upstream repo/PyPI package, or importing/reading an installed copy of the library elsewhere on disk (site-packages, global node modules, absolute user paths, `find /`). You are analyzing past attempts of an AI bug-fixing agent to identify what went wrong in its PROCESS. DO NOT EDIT ANY FILES. DO NOT USE THE NETWORK. All evidence is read-only, in the sandbox working directory under `bundle/failures/<attempt-id>/`.

Each attempt folder contains:
- `report.md` — the bug report given to the agent
- `patch.diff` — the patch the agent submitted (may be empty/absent)
- `trace.md` — narrative of what the agent did
- `commands.md` — every shell command run, each line prefixed with a thread name in brackets (`main` = the agent itself; any other name = a subagent it spawned)
- `result.json` — fields: attempt, bug_class, outcome, bug_tests_passed, failures, how_it_ended. Outcome meanings: `void` = the attempt did not count because the agent fetched this project's code or its fix from the network, or read another copy of the library elsewhere on this machine; `no_patch` = the agent never submitted a patch (often an iteration-limit error in how_it_ended); `f2p_failed` = a patch was submitted but the bug remained.

Your assigned attempt folders (read every one):
1. bundle/failures/round-1-a--boltons-452-backoff-3
2. bundle/failures/run-02--node-semver-512-tilde-2
3. bundle/failures/run-01--node-semver-226-dotted-inc-2
4. bundle/failures/round-1-a--humanize-329-naturalsize-2
5. bundle/failures/run-01--humanize-359-metric-1
6. bundle/failures/run-01--boltons-452-backoff-1
7. bundle/failures/run-01--node-semver-606-diff-3

For each attempt:
1. Read report.md, result.json, trace.md; skim commands.md with `rg`/`sed` (it can be long).
2. Report in at most 4 lines: (a) outcome and how the attempt ended; (b) the specific process failure — what the agent skipped, assumed, reached for, or stopped too early on. Quote the exact command line(s) or trace moment(s) that demonstrate it (especially any command that reads or writes OUTSIDE the working tree `work/repo`, and what the agent was trying to learn when it did that); (c) the ONE general habit that would have prevented it (general — do not name projects, functions, files or tests).

End with a section `COMMON PATTERNS`: the recurring process failures across your assigned attempts, each listed with the attempt ids exhibiting them.

Constraints: never edit files; never run network commands; whole reply under 120 lines; do not paste large code blocks.

===REPORT===
Tilde range with no patch number misses prereleases under includePrerelease

With `includePrerelease` turned on, a tilde range that leaves out the patch number doesn't match a prerelease of the first version in the range. The docs say `~3.4` means the same as `3.4.x`, and the x-range and caret forms both match it.

```js
const semver = require('semver')
const opts = { includePrerelease: true }
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '3.4.*', opts)   // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '>=3.4.*', opts) // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '^3.4.*', opts)  // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '~3.4.*', opts)  // false
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '~3.4', opts)    // false
```

===REPORT===
`semver.inc` resets the prerelease counter when the identifier contains a dot

I bump prereleases with `semver.inc`, passing a dot-separated identifier so the version keeps its two-part tag. The counter never moves. Whatever number the version is on, it goes back to zero:

```js
const semver = require('semver')
semver.inc('5.2.0-rc.next.3', 'prerelease', 'rc.next')
// got:      5.2.0-rc.next.0
// expected: 5.2.0-rc.next.4
```

If I leave the identifier out, the number goes up as it should:

```js
semver.inc('5.2.0-rc.next.3', 'prerelease') // 5.2.0-rc.next.4
```

The version already has that identifier followed by a counter, so I expected the counter to go up, not restart from zero.===TRACE===

===REPORT===
While showing file sizes in a dashboard with `humanize.naturalsize`, I noticed that values sitting just under a unit boundary come out looking wrong. The number rounds up, but the unit doesn't move with it:

```python
>>> from humanize import naturalsize
>>> naturalsize(999_960)
'1000.0 kB'
>>> naturalsize(999_980_000)
'1000.0 MB'
>>> naturalsize(1024**3 - 1, binary=True)
'1024.0 MiB'
```

I expected `'1.0 MB'`, `'1.0 GB'` and `'1.0 GiB'`, which is what you get by passing the round value itself. `gnu=True` output has the same problem at its boundaries. ===REPORT===
backoff_iter crashes on factor=1.0 when count is left out

`backoff_iter` rejects a `factor` below 1.0 with a `ValueError`, so 1.0 looks like valid input. But if I pass exactly 1.0 and leave out `count`, it dies with an unhandled error:

```python
from boltons.iterutils import backoff_iter

list(backoff_iter(2.0, 30.0, factor=1.0))
# ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
```

Giving an explicit `count` works and produces a flat sequence:

```python
list(backoff_iter(2.0, 30.0, count=4, factor=1.0))
# [2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0]
```

A value the function's own validation lets through shouldn't end in a raw `ZeroDivisionError`. A flat sequence can never climb to a larger `stop`, so no count can be worked out here, and I expected a descriptive `ValueError` instead.===TRACE===

1. **Out-of-tree oracles (void)**:61 of 85 failures. Analysts 1 and 2 confirm across tasks: reviewer subagents (and sometimes main) fetched upstream source/issues/fixes over network, or found/read/installed other copies of the library on the machine (global node modules, site-packages, `find /`), often to check correctness. Many attempts PASSED all bug tests yet were voided purely because of this.

2. **no_patch** (22): budget exhaustion — including "endless re-verification until cancelled" which is basically the dropped round-1 change ("bound every optional verification round... go straight to submit"). Don't repeat.

3. **f2p_failed** (2): treating report's literal suggestion as whole spec — only 2 attempts.

So cause: reaching outside the working tree for ground truth (network fetch of project code/fix, or reading/importing other copies of the library elsewhere on the machine) — voids attempts. This is on ≥2 tasks — dozens of tasks.

Notably, the patch-review skill's reviewer brief says "The project is in work/repo... Read the changed code" but the reviewer went beyond — seeking reference implementations. So the rule could be added to the patch-review skill (constrain reviewer) or instructions. Hmm — one idea: add to `patch-review` SKILL.md a constraint: "Tell the reviewer to use only the working tree; it must not fetch code or read other copies of the library." But the cause spans more than reviewers: main agents also did it. The most central place: fix-workflow skill or instructions.

Now step 3: skeptic subagent to check against bundle/passes/. Passes: 12 attempts. Questions: do passing attempts also fetch network / read other copies? If yes → contradiction (would mean void isn't what distinguishes). Actually passes presumably did NOT do that (or would be void). Skeptic should check commands.md/trace.md of passes for network/out-of-tree commands and report whether the passes contradict the cause. Also check: do passes share other habits (e.g., finish quickly) that might suggest alternative cause?

Give skeptic the specific claim to test: "Root cause: attempts failed because they reached outside the working tree — fetching the project's code/tests/fix from the network or reading another copy of the library elsewhere on the machine — which voids the attempt regardless of test results." Test against bundle/passes/*: look for any network/out-of-tree commands; check result.json outcomes (passes have outcome?); report contradicting evidence and any alternative explanation for why passes passed.

Let me dispatch skeptic.
